name: astronomy
title: Astronomy
scope: Intro astronomy for orbits, light-year distances, galaxies, and redshift as a wavelength shift.
method: Sort the question into an orbit, a cosmic distance, or a galaxy-scale pattern.
For an orbit, name the central mass, the period T, and the semi-major axis a.
Apply Kepler's third law: T squared is proportional to a cubed for that same central mass.
Treat a light-year as distance only, the length light travels in one year.
Read redshift as a wavelength shift of a known line toward longer wavelength.
Keep a local orbit and a galaxy redshift on separate scales, and state which one you are using.
Give the relation and its assumption, and do not invent an observation.

formulas.name: Kepler's third law
formulas.use: For one central mass, the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.

formulas.name: Kepler's third law (explicit)
formulas.use: The proportionality constant is 4π squared divided by G times the central mass M.

formulas.name: Light-year
formulas.use: A light-year is a distance of about 9.46 trillion kilometers, not a unit of time.

formulas.name: Redshift
formulas.use: Redshift is the fractional wavelength shift when the observed line is longer than the rest line.

checks: A larger semi-major axis means a longer period, with T scaling as a to the power 3/2.
A light-year answers how far, even though the name contains a year.
Redshift z is positive only when the observed wavelength is longer than the rest wavelength.
Do not use an orbit formula to size a galaxy or a redshift to replace a period.
limits: These are intro relations, not a navigation solution or an observing schedule.
The card does not choose between a motion redshift and cosmic expansion without the scale and the data.
It stays on orbits, distances, galaxies, and redshift, and it is not a sky forecast.
